text: From High Pass, descend into the basin below the peak. Traverse west and ascend boulder fields and scree to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 feet. Locate the gully system in the rocky face with two narrow channels 30 feet apart; take the right channel and ascend the narrow then open gully to broken rock to attain the ridge top. Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the summit. Most of ridge top has a way trail and the route is partially marked with cairns after leaving the basin, but cairns may be far apart and the way trail may disappear for long stretches. If you lose cairns or way trail most gullies probably work though some may be more difficult than others.

A way trail runs along most of the ridge top, and cairns mark part of the route once you are out of the basin, though the cairns can be widely spaced and the trail can vanish for long stretches. Should you lose both, most gullies will probably go, although some are harder than others.

text:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

edits.old: past a good log bridge with a handrail
edits.new: crossing a sturdy log bridge that has a handrail

text: Start at Easy Pass Trailhead at Highway 20 mile 151 (elevation 3,700 ft). Hike 3.5 miles gaining 2,800 feet to Easy Pass (6,500 ft). Descend into Fisher Basin via steep scenic trail through alpine meadows and forest (1.5 miles). Continue to Fisher Creek valley floor and established campsites. From camp area, cross Fisher Creek via large fallen log and travel east side of Douglas Creek valley on faint climber's path. This transition from forest to open terrain is where the route becomes extremely challenging—travelers encounter a vast field of slide alder and other brush, 10+ feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, with small rocky stream channels crisscrossing the ground. Progress is measured in inches per minute. Off-trail navigational skill critical.

edits.new: travelers meet an enormous stretch of slide alder and other brush, 10+ feet high

text: Climb the upper-basin headwall by its weakest line, on the west side a little north of where the glacier hangs down, among waterfalls and brush holds; off-line it becomes class 4. Above the steepest part, traverse level left (south) at about 5,800 ft around a small rock buttress and tree band to the glacier toe. A longer detour around the left side avoids the headwall and may be easier in descent; parties unsure of their line may need a rappel.

edits.new: on the west side, slightly north of the point where the glacier hangs down

text: The 7,300 ft notch is the first proof and the white rock strip is the second. From the broad basin below the peak, turn south along the edge of a steep scree slope dotted with larch and make a beeline through talus and snow for the notch on the southwest ridge at about 7,300 ft. That notch is the gateway; a gap without the scree-and-larch slope leading to it is the wrong one. From the notch, walking up the southwest ridge leads directly into cliffs — this is expected and is not a sign you are off route. The fix is to drop about a hundred feet on grass to get round a buttress, then traverse upward beneath a striking vertical strip of white rock, hugging the edge below an overhang and taking care on the small loose rock lying over sloping slabs. That white band is unmistakable and is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse. Above it, keep scrambling just below the ridgeline rather than following the jagged crest itself, and finish over stacked boulders to the summit block.

edits.old: turn south along the edge of a steep scree slope dotted with larch
edits.new: turn south and follow the rim of a steep scree slope dotted with larch

text: Nothing marks the turn — the tell is what happens if you carry straight on. Past Merritt Lake the maintained trail climbs to the ridge trail; a short way along it an unsigned junction sends the climbers' path uphill toward this peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, no post and no blaze, and parties carrying a track have still needed to hunt for it. The overshoot tell is the useful part: going straight on at that junction descends toward Lost Lake, so losing height toward water means you are past the turn and should come back. Higher, the route gives you the one genuinely visual landmark on the mountain — climb the ridge until the snow gives way to a rocky, jagged, narrow crest, which looks impassable at first glance. The line follows the moat between rock and snow just off to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, then wraps a big rock tower on its right side, staying close in at its base, and scrambles dirt and ledges to a knoll and one last snowfield. The summit above is bare and flat rather than a point, and the register does not sit on the high point but off to the south of the flat area.

edits.old: climb the ridge until the snow gives way to a rocky, jagged, narrow crest
edits.new: keep climbing the ridge until the snow ends and a rocky, jagged, narrow crest takes over

text: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. From there most parties drop back into Leroy Creek Basin to retrieve camp and reverse the Leroy Creek climber's path and Phelps Creek Trail to the trailhead; some parties instead exit via the Ice Lakes basin and the Carne Mountain High Route depending on snow conditions and where camp/vehicles are staged, which several parties describe as an efficient alternative when the Maude/Seven Fingered Jack col has gone soft and mushy in the afternoon. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly reported on the standard descent line (the single technical rappel reported is on the approach traverse under the face, not the summit descent, and is conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route). Descent-specific hazards: loose 3rd-class rock and scree on the south ridge/upper slopes, a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side (stay well back from the edge near the top), lingering steep snow and possible rockfall in the col/gully area, and — if exiting toward Ice Lakes — extra route-finding and a longer, more remote tail to the car. Parties should budget real time for this descent; one party logged roughly 13 hours car-to-car including the North Face climb and this walk-off.

edits.old: a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side
edits.new: a big cornice that builds along the summit ridge over the climber's-right side of the North Face

text: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.

text:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

edits.old: A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose
edits.new: Parties choose the line up a rib on the face's right side

text: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.

text: Approach as for the North Face: Phelps Creek trailhead, the Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the unmarked climbers' trail up the north side of Leroy Creek into the basin, and on up toward Ice Lakes. Parties bivy on ledges above the south side of the lake, below the South Ridge. That is the sensible camp because the South Ridge is the descent — but be clear that it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain for this route, so the morning starts with a long traverse over a cliff band to reach the access notch. One party set themselves a turnaround rule of two hours from camp to the notch, on the grounds that any slower and there would not be time to finish. Cross the talus above the lake to the notch that lets you onto the Entiat Glacier. Rope up and descend to find a short crossing through the ablation zone of the receding glacier — this is harder than the old published photograph suggests. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.

edits.old: Cross the talus above the lake to the notch that lets you onto the Entiat Glacier. Rope up and descend to find a short crossing through the ablation zone
edits.new: Cross the talus above the lake to reach the notch giving access to the Entiat Glacier. Then rope up, descend, and look for a short way across the ablation zone

text:
The notch is the thing you can get wrong, and there is a documented decoy. The access notch is at about 7,200 ft. A climbers' path leads to a different notch at about 6,900 ft, and a party who took it for the right one paid for the error with a long detour in the wrong direction up an ugly scree bash. If the notch you have reached is around six-nine rather than seven-two, keep going.

Once through the correct notch and onto the glacier, the sequence is: descend, cross the ablation zone, pass under the rock spur, then work rightward beneath the headwall. Arrival at the climbing is a change in the ice — you move from walking to big crevasses with short vertical steps, and above those the angle relaxes to about thirty-five degrees of ice running up to the base of the rock.

That base of rock is the second, unmistakable transition: roughly nine hundred feet of fourth and low fifth class above it, with several ramps to choose between. Take the line of least resistance trending slightly toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method rather than pitching it. There is a distinctive step-across at the top of a couloir partway up.

A note on how much ice you will actually find: in a heavy snow year one party bypassed roughly two pitches of the icefall on steep snow slopes off to the side, and the whole icefall took them an hour of running belays where they had budgeted six. Do not plan the day around a pitch count from an older description.

Descent is the South Ridge, which took that party half an hour — which is exactly why the camp is where it is.

edits.new: paid for it with an ugly scree bash, a long detour heading the wrong way

edits.old: Take the line of least resistance trending slightly toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly
edits.new: Follow the line of least resistance, angling a little toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly

edits.new: Partway up, at the top of a couloir, you meet a distinctive step across.

text: Descend loose shower-tile scree on the far side to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin, drop into the basin and cross a dark moraine to the jade-green lake at the foot of the Mystery Glacier.

text: Get onto the Mystery Glacier at its lower left corner and cross it diagonally, trending right, to the col at about 6,700 ft on the peak's east side. From the col traverse mixed rock and snow to open snow about 200 ft south, climb it staying south of the blocky rock band, and continue up loose rock to the notch, trending climber's left as you approach it.

text:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet; an overnight stay needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. A short way up, stay left where the Maynard Burn Way branches off; it is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp, about 4 miles in, is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.

edits.old: then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin
edits.new: then go down shower-tile scree onto grass and heather benches overlooking Deception Basin

text:
The base of the climb is the lower left corner of the Mystery Glacier, and the thing that marks it is a lake you cannot mistake for anything else: a jade-green moraine-bounded lake sits at the glacier's base. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its lower left corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

The test for the glacier crossing is a diagonal: you enter at the lower left and exit at the upper right, at a col at about 6,700 ft on the peak's east side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

Second test, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach open snow about 200 ft south of the col, then climb those slopes staying south of the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

Third test, and it is the commitment point: a short class 4 step on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a notch near 7,500 ft. Trend climber's left on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

What confirms you are through: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and the rock gets markedly better than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.

edits.old: a jade-green moraine-bounded lake sits at the glacier's base
edits.new: at the glacier's base lies a lake of jade green, bounded by moraine

text: Beyond the notch a clean class 3 gully leads to the summit block, where the rock is markedly better than anything below and the line to the 7,639 ft top is obvious. The peak is sometimes given an overall class 3 rating by the easiest line, with the 4th class step being the deciding feature; unavoidable loose rock, scree and dirt with exposure characterize the whole ascent regardless of the rating.

edits.old: unavoidable loose rock, scree and dirt with exposure characterize the whole ascent regardless of the rating
edits.new: loose rock, scree and dirt that cannot be avoided, along with exposure, mark the entire ascent whatever its rating

text: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. The eastern Six Ridge Trail is closed from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail, and has been since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026; that leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead, over Sundown Pass, as the way in.

edits.new: On the eastern Six Ridge Trail, the stretch from the east edge of Belview Camp down to the North Fork Skokomish trail junction is closed

text: Descend the same North Ridge/Blue Glacier line in reverse. From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock, the roughly Class 4 with one Class 5 (5.4-ish) step is reversed by rappel rather than downclimbed by most parties: build/clip the fixed summit anchor (recent parties note slung horns/blocks and a semi-permanent thin rappel line has appeared in some seasons, though this should not be trusted blindly) and rappel the north side of the summit block. A single-strand rappel with a 40-50m rope reaches the notch/belay ledge for most of the season; a 60m rope (doubled, ~30m per strand) is the safer bet as summer progresses and snow recedes below the block, and some parties join two ropes to make one long rappel to the base of the block instead of two shorter ones. An alternative is a single-rope rappel off the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then downclimbing the original route. Anchor material is a mix of fixed slings on horns/chockstones and natural gear (small cams in the 0.3-0.4 range have been used to back up or build anchors) rather than bolts — inspect any in-place tat before trusting it. Below the summit block, reverse the snow slope (mind the runout) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the Blue Glacier crossing, regain the lateral moraine catwalk, and retrace the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles back to the trailhead, watching for the ladder/washout section and any lingering steep snow between Glacier Meadows and Elk Lake.

edits.old: From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock
edits.new: Starting at the foot of the summit rock, about 80 ft tall

text:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because the true summit is not visible from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is east of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the left, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

edits.new: ends up on the five-fingered false summit, sitting east of its real target

edits.old: there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4
edits.new: there is also a line of about 80 ft directly up the north face over rock that is mostly solid, around 5.4

text: The path begins on the north side of the creek where the road fords it, and follows the north bank through old growth, boulders and windfall. The brush thickens, then the path makes a rising traverse into a rocky gully; climb that gully — talus, sometimes snow-filled — to a small basin at about 4,300 ft. Fix that basin in mind, because on the way down it is the aiming point before you drop back to the creek and losing it puts you in the wrong drainage. From it, continue straight up and then cut left up a second gully into the basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft. That upper basin is the base of the climb proper, and two lines leave it for the south ridge: a centre gully, and a left-hand one giving 45 to 50 degree snow followed by a short loose, brushy Class 4 rock step. The presence of that step is how you know which gully you are in. Once on the crest the going is Class 2 to 3 with one genuinely knife-edged section, and the true high point is the south peak of three.

edits.new: cut left up a second gully, reaching the basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft

text: From the Verlot Public Service Center on the Mountain Loop Highway, continue east about 4.6 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 4020 (Schweitzer Creek Road, signed for Boardman Lake/Ashland Lakes/Bear-Pinnacle Lake). Follow FR 4020 for 2.7 miles to a junction, take the right fork onto FR 4021, and continue 1.4 miles on a rough road to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead (about 2,700 ft; small ~15-car lot, no toilet). Hike the Pinnacle Lake Trail to the lake, walk around its southwest shore to Iodine Creek, and follow the creek up through Iodine Gulch to its top; turn right and continue a short distance to the Bathtub Lakes basin. From there, continue scrambling west to reach Mount Pilchuck's summit.

text: The off-trail climbing starts at the southwest shore of the lake, where the maintained tread ends and the creek enters. Walk round the lake to that corner and pick up the creek — the creek line is the route from there, because there is nothing else. Follow it up through the gulch to its top; two distinct steep steps inside the gulch are the crux of the day and are the confirmation you are in the right drainage. At the top of the gulch, turn right and continue a short distance to the basin holding the small lakes, then scramble west to reach the summit. Negative markers: if you are still on continuous, obviously maintained trail, you have not left it yet — the trail does not go beyond the lake; and if you are crossing an open boulder field following orange painted blazes toward a fixed steel ladder, you have come up the peak's standard trail from the opposite side of the mountain.

edits.old: turn right and continue a short distance to the basin holding the small lakes
edits.new: bear right and go a short way farther to the basin holding the small lakes

text: Descend the trail steeply about 0.8 mile to a gravel service road, go left briefly, then turn right down to Ross Dam. Cross the dam and follow the trail north along the west shore of Ross Lake about 6 miles to Big Beaver Creek and the Big Beaver Trail junction. A water taxi to Big Beaver Landing skips this shoreline stretch.

text: Mount Queets (6,476 ft) is a remote summit in the interior Olympic Mountains, sitting on the divide near the headwaters of both the Elwha and Queets rivers, just southwest of the Bailey Range and Dodwell-Rixon Pass. It is built of Eocene basalt, and heavy winter snowfall sustains the small Queets Glacier in a cirque on its north slope despite the peak's modest elevation. Harry Fisher (recorded as James B. Hanmore) and Nelson Linsley made the first recorded ascent in 1890 during the Army's O'Neil Expedition. There is no maintained trail to the peak; it lies deep in Olympic National Park wilderness and is normally climbed either as a side objective from the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse or via a dedicated cross-country backpack up the Elwha River to Elwha Basin.

text: There is no direct trailhead-to-summit trail. Vehicle access to the Elwha Valley has been closed since a May 2021 washout on Olympic Hot Springs Road; you now walk or bike an extra ~6-7 miles from the Madison Falls parking area (past the washout, then up Whiskey Bend Road) just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead. From Whiskey Bend, follow the Elwha River Trail to Chicago Camp, where it fords the Elwha short of Low Divide, then leave the trail and continue about 3 miles cross-country up into Elwha Basin and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763 ft) to reach the north ridge of Mount Queets. Most parties treat this as a multi-day (4+ day round trip) wilderness objective, commonly combined with the Bailey Range Traverse via Queets Basin to the west. The lower third of the north ridge is mostly 2nd-class scrambling on crumbly rock and heather; where it becomes impassable, drop a few hundred feet to traverse steep, firm scree around 5,300 ft on the east side to bypass a cliff band, then regain the ridge for an easy 2nd-class scramble around its west side before a moderately steep snow slope on the east side leads to the summit. Microspikes and an axe have been used here even in late August.

text: Dodwell-Rixon Pass is the divide between the Elwha and Queets drainages, with a small tarn just below it and Mount Olympus in view to the west. The north ridge is gained directly from the pass, so the base is the pass itself and the lower third of the ridge is straightforward Class 2 on crumbly rock and steep heather with brushy patches. The identification that matters is where to leave the crest. About a third of the way along, the ridge ahead becomes impassable; the move is to drop a couple of hundred feet off the east side onto steep, firm scree and traverse. Hold that traverse until you have passed below a steep cliff roughly halfway along the east side of the ridge, then climb back up talus, steep heather and crumbly slabs to regain the crest for the final third. From there it is easy Class 2 around the west side of the ridge, then a moderately steep snow slope on the east side to the top — snow that has needed an axe here even in late August. If you are still on the crest and the rock ahead of you is vertical, you have missed the drop-off point and should go back for it.

text: From White River Campground (reached via WA-410 and White River Road — check the park's current road status for early/late-season openings), hike the Glacier Basin Trail roughly 3.5 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Glacier Basin (~5,900 ft), a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camping spot. From there, continue on climbers' path up to St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), gaining another ~1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree/snow. At St. Elmo Pass, rope up for glacier travel: drop down onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west/southwest, threading around crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east (Winthrop) side. This is the same approach corridor used for Liberty Ridge, so expect other parties and established boot tracks in season. Above St. Elmo Pass there is no water; carry enough for the climb or plan to melt snow.

text:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,700 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.

text: Cross the Nisqually Glacier roped from the moraine and climb the Wilson gully (rockfall) onto the Wilson Glacier. Follow its left edge to about 9,000 ft, then cut right toward the cleaver between the Wilson and Nisqually, where camps sit around 9,100–9,500 ft. From camp cross the upper Wilson Glacier to the foot of the couloir; debris from the Kautz Ice Cliff can reach this ground.

text: The historic 1870 Stevens-Van Trump first-ascent route, traversing exposed ledges beneath the cliff of Gibraltar Rock on the south side. From Camp Muir the route ascends the western edge of the Cowlitz Glacier below the Cowlitz Cleaver, passes beneath a rock feature called the Beehive, and crosses the cleaver through a notch to reach the base of Gibraltar Rock. From about 11,800 ft the route follows exposed snow-and-rock 'ledges' along the base of Gibraltar Rock for roughly a third of a mile to the top of Gibraltar Chute (~12,600 ft, sometimes called 'Camp Comfort'); the crux is an ice chute between Gibraltar Rock and the upper Nisqually ice cliff leading to the saddle. From there it's a sustained ~2,000 ft push to the east crater rim and across the crater to the true summit.

text:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.

text:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts below Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be losing height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

text: From the summit area, traverse the upper Winthrop Glacier beneath Columbia Crest and pick up the Emmons-Winthrop route down to Camp Schurman at Steamboat Prow. Cross the prow and descend the Inter Glacier into Glacier Basin, then follow the trail out to the White River trailhead. This returns to the trailhead you started from, but it does not retrace the approach: the St. Elmo Pass, Curtis Ridge and Carbon Glacier leg is not reversed. Do not plan on downclimbing Liberty Ridge itself. Parties who instead carry over the summit and descend the Disappointment Cleaver to Camp Muir finish at Paradise, a different trailhead that needs a car shuttle.

text:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

edits.new: That is your cue to move left across into a snow face shaped like an hourglass, not to keep going up.

text: Sunset Ridge climbs the long spine separating the upper Mowich Face from the Sunset Amphitheater on Rainier's remote west/northwest side. After the long Westside Road/Wonderland Trail approach to St. Andrews Park, the route climbs a series of steep 50-55° gullies and open faces; at about 12,800 ft the ridge forces climbers out onto the upper Mowich Face, which is followed on steep snow or ice to 13,200 ft before the route regains the ridge crest to Liberty Cap and the true summit. It's a long, committing outing best suited to fast parties comfortable with routefinding on glaciated, seldom-traveled terrain.

text: A classic, remote west-side glacier route. From the toe of the Tahoma Glacier the route ascends a series of diagonal zigzags — first up the glacier's south side to about 7,200 ft, then traversing to the opposite (north) side by ~9,000 ft, with further traverses between sides up to roughly 10,000 ft. Above that, climbers turn north to about 11,200 ft to enter the 'Sickle,' a steep chute at the extreme left (north) edge of the glacier used to bypass the icefall below; it's climbed on its north side, keeping left of icy ridges, to a plateau around 12,600 ft, from which the route joins the upper mountain.

text: The Sickle is the chute on the far left (north) edge of the glacier that bypasses the central icefall. Climb it on its north side, keeping left of the icy ridges, to a plateau at about 12,600 ft. Ice avalanches from the summit ice cap sweep this chute; climb it early and cold, and treat it as a no-go when there is fresh debris or warm conditions.

text: A notorious roughly 4,000-ft north face — the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's cirque — capped by a 200-300 ft band of hanging ice (seracs) that has historically deterred most attempts and is the wall's defining objective hazard. Named for geological engineer Bailey Willis, who helped build the first trail to the Carbon Glacier in 1881. The wall's West Rib was first climbed in June 1961 by Charles ('Charlie') Bell, though credit for the first ascent was disputed for years; Jim Wickwire (who climbed the East Rib in 1963 and made the first winter ascent in 1970) later corroborated Bell's claim by comparing notes and photographs directly with Bell.
